area: Area IV. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can fly a stabilized approach at the published speed (or not more than 1.3 VSO) within 5 knots, correct for gusts and crosswind, use VASI/PAPI guidance against visual illusions, and touch down on or within 200 feet past a chosen point, going around early whenever the approach is not working.
why: The landing phase accounts for more pilot-caused accidents than any other single phase of flight [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. As a commercial pilot you will land with passengers on short, wet, gusty and unfamiliar runways, where small errors in speed or height quickly use up the runway [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]].

warmup: Your POH approach speed is 70 kt. The wind is gusting, the runway is narrow and wet, and the examiner wants you on the aiming point markings. Which single number on final will decide whether you make the 200-foot box, and at what point would you give up and go around?

key_terms.def: Stalling speed or minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration.
Final approach speed to use when the manufacturer gives none; the ACS ceiling in that case.
Gust speed minus steady wind speed. Pilots often add half of it to approach speed.
A constant-angle glide path to a chosen point at constant airspeed and configuration.
Where the glide path would meet the ground with no flare. It does not move in the windshield.
Precision Approach Path Indicator: a row of 2 or 4 lights showing red and white for glide path.
Visual Approach Slope Indicator: bars of red/white lights giving visual descent guidance.
Rudder holds the nose on centerline; upwind wing lowered just enough to stop drift.
Heading turned into the wind so the track follows centerline; crab removed with rudder at touchdown.
Crosswind shown controllable in certification testing; at least 0.2 VSO, placarded since 1962.
Available Landing Distance: runway length to the hold-short point for a LAHSO clearance.
Running off the far end because speed, height, tailwind or surface used up the runway.

chunks.title: The commercial standard and the five phases

body.p: You already land well. At the commercial level the examiner wants the same landing flown tighter: a precise speed, a precise spot, and an early go-around when either one slips. The AFH splits the end of every landing into five phases: base leg, final approach, round out (flare), touchdown, and after-landing roll [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

body.p: A normal approach assumes engine power is available, the wind is light or straight down the runway, there are no obstacles on final, and the runway is firm and long enough to stop gradually. The selected landing point is normally past the threshold but within the first third of the runway [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. Your POH speeds and configurations come first: the AFH says the manufacturer's procedures take precedence over its general guidance [[24:172|AFH 9-1]].

The aiming point is where the glide path would meet the ground if you never flared. You actually touch down past it, because the round out slows your descent and you float a little. Allowing for that float lets you predict the touchdown point with some accuracy [[24:175|AFH 9-4]] [[24:176|AFH 9-5]]. For the 200-foot box, that is the whole game: know your float, then pick the aiming point that puts the wheels on the examiner's spot.

callout.text: Before-landing checklist (and gear down, if retractable) is normally done before you reach base leg [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. The after-landing checklist waits until you are clear of the runway and stopped [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].
No crosswind on checkride day? The examiner must test your crosswind knowledge orally (ACS CA.IV.B note). Know this lesson's crosswind chunks cold.

check.q: The examiner names the first touchdown zone marker as your point. Where may your wheels touch?
check.a: On it or up to 200 feet beyond it, in landing attitude, with no drift and aligned over the centerline (ACS CA.IV.B.S10).

body.p: A stabilized approach is a constant-angle glide path to a chosen point on the runway, flown at a constant final descent airspeed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. It makes the round out, touchdown and rollout much easier and cuts the chance of a landing mishap, so catch deviations early while the corrections are still small [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

Energy management means pitch and power together. Going to overshoot: reduce power and lower the nose to keep airspeed, or add flaps if you have some left. Going to undershoot: add power and raise the nose together to shallow the descent [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Raising the nose alone to stretch the glide raises the angle of attack and bleeds airspeed, which leads to a high sink rate or a low-altitude stall [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

bullets: Low and on the backside of the power curve? Leveling off to meet the glide path may need a big power increase. When you meet the path, reduce power and pitch down to stay on it [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].
Never raise the flaps to fix an undershoot. It causes a sudden loss of lift, a big sink rate, and a worse approach [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].
Trim off the pressures once set up, then scan: aiming point, horizon, objects along the runway, an area well short of the runway, and back. Glance at the airspeed indicator often [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

callout.text: Gates: not stabilized by 500 ft above airport elevation in VMC, or 1,000 ft in IMC, means go around. In a typical piston pattern, go around immediately if the approach goes unstable below 300 ft AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].
The AFH airspeed window (+10/-5) is a stabilization gate. Your checkride window is tighter: ±5 kt (ACS CA.IV.B.S7). Fly to the tighter one.

check.q: You are low and a bit slow on a 1-mile final. What is the right fix, and what is the wrong one?
check.a: Right: add power and raise the nose to level off at the correct airspeed, then reduce power and pitch down when you meet the glide path. Wrong: pulling back alone, or raising the flaps [[24:177|AFH 9-6]] [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

chunks.title: Approach speed, gust factor, and flaps

body.p: On final, use the manufacturer's recommended speed, or 1.3 VSO if there is none [[24:174|AFH 9-3]]. VSO is the stalling speed in the landing configuration; on base leg the AFH target is about 1.4 VSO [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. The ACS uses the same ceiling: the published speed, or not more than 1.3 VSO, held within ±5 kt (ACS CA.IV.B.S7).
Multipliers from [[24:173|AFH 9-2]] and [[24:174|AFH 9-3]].

Gusts and turbulence: fly a power-on approach slightly faster than normal for more positive control. Pilots often use normal speed plus half the gust factor. The AFH example: normal 70 kt with 15 kt gusts gives about 77 kt [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. The gust factor is the gust value minus the steady wind: wind 18 gusting 28 is a 10-kt gust factor, so add 5 kt. The ACS then wants that adjusted target held ±5 kt (ACS CA.IV.B.S7).

bullets: Use partial flaps in a gusty crosswind. The higher pitch attitude needs less pitch change to land, and you touch down a little faster with better control [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].
Keep enough power to hold speed and path. Close the throttle only after the mains touch; chopping it early in turbulence can cause a hard landing [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].
In turbulence you touch down in about a level attitude; avoid forward pressure afterward, which can cause wheelbarrowing [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].
If you apply a gust factor, do not let indicated airspeed decay below the recommended landing speed [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

body.p: Flaps add lift and drag. They allow slower speeds, a steeper descent, a lower nose for better view, and a shorter roll [[24:172|AFH 9-1]]. Up to about 15 degrees mostly adds lift (expect a balloon); beyond 15 degrees adds a lot of drag. Extend them in steps on downwind, base and final so the pitch and power changes stay small, and re-trim each time. Full flaps are not recommended until final is established [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

callout.text: The gust additive is not permission to be fast. As a rule of thumb, a 10 percent faster final approach gives a 20 percent longer landing distance [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]].

check.q: POH approach speed 65 kt. Wind 240 at 10 gusting 24. What is your target, and what window must you hold?
check.a: Gust factor 14 kt, half is 7: target 72 kt [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Hold 67 to 77 kt (ACS CA.IV.B.S7), never below 65 kt [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

body.p: A VASI uses red and white light beams: each unit shows white in the upper part of its beam and red in the lower part. A 2-bar VASI gives one glide path, normally 3 degrees. It is visible 3 to 5 miles by day and 20 miles or more at night, and gives safe obstruction clearance within 10 degrees of the extended centerline out to 4 NM [[33:121|AIM 2-1-2]]. On a 2-bar VASI, all red means below the path, red over white means on it, and all white means above it [[33:123|AIM 2-1-2]].

A PAPI uses similar light units in a single row of two or four, normally on the left side of the runway. It is visible about 5 miles by day and 20 miles at night, with obstruction clearance within 10 degrees of centerline out to 3.4 NM. With either system, do not start the descent until you are visually lined up with the runway [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2]] [[33:121|AIM 2-1-2]].

Source for the table: [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2]]. Some glide paths are as steep as 4.5 degrees for obstacles; angles over 3.5 degrees can increase the runway needed for landing and rollout [[33:121|AIM 2-1-2]].

callout.text: At an airport in Class D airspace, an airplane landing on a runway served by a visual approach slope indicator must stay at or above the glide path until a lower altitude is necessary for a safe landing. Normal bracketing to stay on the path is allowed [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(e)(3)-(4)]].

body.p: No lights? The AIM's 3-to-1 rule nearly duplicates a 3-degree path: 3,000 ft at 10 miles, 1,500 ft at 5 miles, 1,200 ft at 4 miles, and so on to touchdown [[34:153|AIM 7-4-8]]. That is about 300 ft per mile. Close in, a 3-degree path is only about 105 ft high at 1,600 ft from the threshold [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].

check.q: At 2 miles the PAPI shows one white and three red. What is your path, and how do you fix it?
check.a: Slightly low, about 2.8 degrees [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2]]. Add power and raise the nose together until you see two white and two red [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

chunks.title: Round out, touchdown accuracy, and rollout

body.p: Where you look matters. Keep your head natural and slowly move your focus from just over the nose to the touchdown zone and back. Focus too close and you over-control, round out high and drop in; focus too far and you react late and may fly into the runway nose first [[24:178|AFH 9-7]]. As the flare starts, look ahead at a shallow 10 to 15 degree angle to the runway [[24:178|AFH 9-7]].

Start the round out about 10 to 20 feet above the ground, raising the nose slowly so the airplane keeps settling as it slows. Reach landing attitude and touchdown speed at the same moment the wheels touch. With full flaps the nose has farther to travel, so raise it a bit faster [[24:179|AFH 9-8]]. Once the flare starts, never push forward; relax or hold the back pressure, and add a little power if sinking too fast. Keep a hand on the throttle the whole time [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].

Touch down on the main wheels at or just above stalling speed. A good habit is to hold the wheels a few inches off as long as possible while power comes smoothly to idle. Never fly the airplane onto the runway with excess speed. The longitudinal axis must be parallel to your path: no touchdown while crabbed or drifting [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].

Accuracy aids: the runway aiming point marking is two broad white stripes about 1,000 feet from the threshold, and touchdown zone markings are coded in 500-foot steps [[33:139|AIM 2-3-3]]. Examiners often use them as the specified point. The enemy of accuracy is float, and float comes from excess speed on final [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]. If the airplane is in landing attitude and only slightly high, hold the attitude and add just enough power to ease it on [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].

bullets: After touchdown, hold back pressure for aerodynamic braking and keep the nose wheel off; make sure no brake pressure is on at touchdown [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].
Let the nose wheel down gently, then brake once directional control is established. Best braking is just short of a skid; pumping the brakes does not help [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].
The landing is not over until you are at taxi speed or stopped clear of the runway. Positively identify the flap control before moving it [[24:180|AFH 9-9]] [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

callout.text: Spot landings start on final, not in the flare. Speed on target means little float, so the aiming point you choose stays where you expect [[24:203|AFH 9-32]] [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].

check.q: Mid-flare, the airplane seems to stop descending, too high. What do you do?
check.a: Hold the pitch attitude until it starts to settle, then continue the round out; add a little power if speed is dropping. If the nose would need to be lowered a lot, go around [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].

chunks.title: Crosswind technique: crab, wing-low, and the rollout

body.p: There are two usual methods: crab and wing-low (sideslip). The crab may be easier to hold on final, but removing it just before touchdown takes judgment and precise timing. The wing-low method is recommended in most cases, a combination is allowed, and current testing standards accept either, so learn both [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

Crab: make a coordinated turn into the wind so the wings-level ground track follows centerline. Hold it until just before touchdown, then use rudder to line the nose up with the runway. Too early or too late puts a side load on the gear. On a long final you can crab first, then change smoothly to wing-low before the round out [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

Wing-low: use rudder to line the nose up with the runway, watch which way you drift, and lower the upwind wing with aileron just enough to stop it. Change the bank to move left or right onto the centerline [[24:187|AFH 9-16]]. A stronger crosswind needs more bank and considerable opposite rudder [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

bullets: As you slow in the flare, the controls lose effect. Keep increasing aileron and rudder to hold the same correction, and keep the upwind wing down all the way [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].
Wing-low touchdown is on the upwind main wheel first; the downwind main settles as you slow. In gusts, adjust the correction promptly so there is no drift at touchdown [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].
With rudder-linked nose wheel steering, relax the rudder as the nose wheel touches so you do not swerve [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].
On the rollout the airplane weathervanes into the wind. Steer with rudder or nose wheel steering, keep adding aileron into the wind, and hold it fully into the wind as you stop [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

Touching down while drifting creates a side load; as little as 10 degrees of cornering angle gives a side load of half the weight on that tire and can roll a tricycle-gear airplane over. Ailerons, rudder and nose wheel steering can prevent it; brakes cannot [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

callout.text: If full opposite rudder cannot stop the turn while you hold the bank you need, the wind is too strong for that runway. Land on a better runway or at an alternate airport [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

check.q: Crosswind from the left, wing-low method. Which wing is down, which rudder is in, and which wheel touches first?
check.a: Left wing down, right rudder to keep the nose on centerline, left main wheel first [[24:187|AFH 9-16]] [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

body.p: Before type certification, an airplane must be shown controllable, without exceptional skill, in a 90-degree crosswind up to 0.2 VSO. For VSO 50 kt that is 10 kt. Airplanes certificated after May 3, 1962 show the demonstrated crosswind on a placard. You must know the maximum crosswind component of every airplane you fly and stay within it [[24:190|AFH 9-19]].

Use a crosswind component chart to split the reported wind into headwind and crosswind parts [[24:190|AFH 9-19]]. Find the angle between the wind and the runway, follow that line out to the wind speed arc, then read straight down for the crosswind component and straight across for the headwind component. Example: runway 27, wind 300 at 20 kt is a 30-degree angle, about 10 kt of crosswind and about 17 kt of headwind.

Treat the demonstrated value with care. Most airplanes publish only a demonstrated crosswind, not a maximum limit, and on a wet or contaminated runway tire cornering limits reduce braking, so crosswind can become the deciding factor [[27:19|AC 91-79B 3.10]].

Runway selection (R1) starts before takeoff: for every flight you must know runway lengths at airports of intended use and your POH takeoff and landing distance data [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]]. On a wet runway, pick the runway most aligned with the wind [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]]. If the crosswind is beyond your skill or the airplane, a different runway or airport is the commercial answer [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

callout.text: 0.2 VSO is the certification test wind, not a guarantee. Your limit is the lower of the placard and your own skill [[24:190|AFH 9-19]].

check.q: VSO is 55 kt. What crosswind did certification testing have to show was controllable?
check.a: 0.2 x 55 = 11 kt, at 90 degrees to the runway [[24:190|AFH 9-19]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step to commercial tolerances

body.p: Generic AFH flow. Use your POH speeds, flap settings and checklists.

bullets: 1. Before the pattern: brief the runway, wind, gust additive, crosswind component, landing distance and exit taxiway. Monitor CTAF from about 10 miles [[24:177|AFH 9-6]] [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.1]].
2. Downwind: before-landing checklist (gear down if retractable) complete before base; radio call [[24:173|AFH 9-2]] [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].
3. Base: reduce power, about 1.4 VSO, flaps as recommended, crab to hold a square ground track. Place base closer in for a strong headwind on final or steep flap setting [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].
4. Turn final coordinated; no skid. Line up and confirm runway number and alignment; scan the runway and nearby area for traffic and obstructions [[24:125|AFH 5-20]] [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].
5. Final flaps, pitch and power for the POH speed (or 1.3 VSO) plus any gust additive; trim. Choose the aiming point that puts touchdown on the specified point [[24:174|AFH 9-3]] [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].
6. Stabilized by 500 ft AGL: on the PAPI/VASI or 3-to-1 path, speed ±5 kt, crosswind held with wing-low [[24:177|AFH 9-6]] [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].
7. At 10 to 20 ft, round out smoothly, power to idle (in gusts, only after the mains touch), more control as you slow [[24:179|AFH 9-8]] [[24:191|AFH 9-20]] [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].
8. Touch down on the mains in landing attitude, no drift, aligned on centerline [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].
9. Rollout: back pressure, aileron into the wind, steer with rudder, brake after the nose wheel is down [[24:181|AFH 9-10]] [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].
10. Exit at the first available taxiway, stop once past the holding position markings, then do the after-landing checklist [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]] [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].
Any step not working: go around (power, attitude, configuration) [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

head: What the examiner checks

check.q: POH speed 70 kt, wind calm. At 300 ft your speed reads 77 kt. Within the ACS window?
check.a: No. Calm wind means no gust additive, so the window is 65 to 75 kt (ACS CA.IV.B.S7). Reduce power and correct now, or go around if it will not settle in time [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

body.p: Terrain features and weather can fool your eyes about height and distance, and these illusions mostly strike on landing [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]. Most of them make you fly a lower approach, and a low approach near the ground is how airplanes hit obstacles or land short.

head: Condition
You feel

rows: Low approach; may hit objects or land short

Featureless terrain, water, darkness, snow (black hole)
Farther and higher than you are

body.p: Sources for the table: [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]] [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]].

bullets: Expect illusions at unfamiliar airports, at night, or in bad weather; check the airport diagram and Chart Supplement for slope, terrain and lighting [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]] [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].
Check the altimeter often on every approach, day and night [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].
Use VASI, PAPI or an electronic glideslope whenever available [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].

body.p: CFIT is one of the top four causes of fatal GA accidents; flying intentionally too low and flying at night are listed causes [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. Stall/spin near the ground: the classic is a base-to-final overshoot with an unrecognized tailwind on base, then more bank, back pressure and inside rudder. That skidding cross-control stall can roll toward inverted and start a spin. The safest action for an overshoot is a go-around [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. A spin from cross-controls usually rotates in the direction of the rudder applied [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]].

check.q: Night, unfamiliar airport, dark terrain short of the runway, and the runway is narrower than you are used to. Which way will you tend to err?
check.a: Low. Both illusions make you feel higher than you are. Use the PAPI or VASI and cross-check the altimeter [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]] [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].

chunks.title: Tailwind, wind shear, surface, and runway overruns

body.p: AC 91-79B lists the hazards that turn a normal landing into an overrun. The first is an unstabilized approach: big deviations in speed, altitude, descent rate, glide path or aim point leave you unlikely to recover. You are responsible for telling ATC when an instruction would force an unstabilized approach [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.1]].

head: Factor
Effect on landing distance
rows: Each 10 ft above the 50 ft threshold height
About 200 ft longer (100 ft crossing height = +1,000 ft) [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]]
Touching down beyond the intended point
POH distance may not be achievable [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.4]]
About 5% faster landing speed and 10% longer distance [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.6]]
5,000 ft density altitude vs sea level

body.p: These add up, and together they can exceed the runway you have [[27:36|AC 91-79B 5.2.10]]. Plan a margin: AC 91-79B uses at least 15 percent on top of the computed landing distance [[27:19|AC 91-79B 3.8.1]]. Since wheel brakes stop you far better than air drag, getting onto the ground at the intended point and braking early shortens the total distance [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.8.1]].

Surface: water reduces braking, and in dynamic hydroplaning the tires ride on a sheet of water with almost no braking or steering [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]]. Minimum hydroplaning speed is about 9 times the square root of the main tire pressure; 36 psi gives 54 kt. Landing faster than recommended raises the risk, and once started, hydroplaning can continue well below that speed [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]]. A slippery runway plus a tailwind is especially risky [[27:18|AC 91-79B 3.7]]. Upslope shortens the landing roll; downslope lengthens it; slope is in the Chart Supplement [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].

Wind shear is a sudden change in wind speed or direction over a small area. A headwind changing to a tailwind cuts airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. A microburst on approach can give a headwind, then a downdraft, then a tailwind that forces you to the ground short of the runway; virga with an intense rain shaft or a ring of blowing dust may be the only clue [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

bullets: Any rapid, large airspeed gain near convective weather may mean a loss is coming, and can be a reason to stop the approach [[28:273|AWH 22-18]].
An increasing headwind shear can also reduce your normal slowdown in the flare and lead to an overrun [[28:273|AWH 22-18]].
Microbursts are often lopsided, so the early airspeed gain may be small or missing [[28:266|AWH 22-11]].
Be ready to go around at the first sign; some microbursts cannot be escaped with any known technique [[28:266|AWH 22-11]].

check.q: POH landing distance 1,500 ft. You must land with a 10 kt tailwind. Roughly how far, before any margin?

body.p: Every aircraft making lift trails two counter-rotating vortices. They can roll an airplane harder than its ailerons can fight [[34:147|AIM 7-4-1]]. Strength grows with weight and falls with speed; the strongest come from aircraft that are HEAVY, CLEAN, and SLOW [[34:147|AIM 7-4-3]]. Short-wingspan airplanes like yours have the hardest time countering the roll [[34:148|AIM 7-4-3]].

bullets: Vortices exist from rotation to touchdown, so note the touchdown or rotation point of the aircraft ahead [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]].
They sink several hundred feet per minute. Fly at or above the preceding aircraft's path [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]].
Within 100 to 200 ft of the ground they spread sideways at 2 or 3 knots [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]].
A 1 to 5 knot crosswind can keep the upwind vortex in the touchdown zone; a tailwind can push vortices forward into it. The light quartering tailwind requires maximum caution [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]].

head: Situation

rows: Stay at or above its final approach path, note its touchdown point, land beyond it

Consider drift to your runway; stay at or above its path; note its touchdown point
Note its rotation point; land well before it
Rotates past the intersection: continue, land before the intersection. Rotates before it: avoid flight below its path; abandon unless landing well before the intersection
After its low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go
Wait at least 2 minutes before landing

body.p: Source for the table: [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

On a visual approach behind a heavy, fly on or above its glide path, using a VASI, ILS or the 3-to-1 rule. With the jet and runway in sight, pick a landing point no less than 1,000 ft from the arrival end, keep your line of sight to it above and in front of the jet, and adjust after you see where it lands [[34:153|AIM 7-4-8]]. Accepting traffic information, an instruction to follow, or a visual approach means you accept wake separation responsibility [[34:153|AIM 7-4-8]]. Warning or not, you are expected to adjust your flight path to avoid a serious encounter [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

callout.text: Above its path, beyond its touchdown, before its rotation, and 2 minutes after its touch-and-go.

check.q: A larger airplane departs on the crossing runway and rotates before it reaches your intersection. What now?
check.a: Avoid flying below its flight path, and abandon the approach unless you can land well before the intersection [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

body.p: A go-around is a normal maneuver for when the approach or landing deviates from what you expect or becomes hazardous: ATC request, something on the runway, overtaking traffic, wind shear, wake turbulence, a mechanical problem, or an unstable approach [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. It is dangerous only when delayed or done poorly. The two causes of delay are landing expectancy ("it will work out") and pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

head: Step
What to do
rows: Full or maximum allowable power, smoothly and without hesitation; carburetor heat off, as applicable [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Don't pitch up without airspeed; you may need to lower the nose briefly. Forward pressure to hold the nose, right rudder for torque and P-factor, rough trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Flaps up in small steps as speed builds; gear up only after a positive rate of climb [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]

body.p: Close to the ground, ground effect lends you performance by reducing induced drag. Climbing out of it too soon can leave you unable to climb, even at full power [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

bullets: Speed outside ±5 kt of target, or the 200-ft box out of reach (ACS CA.IV.B.S11).
Unstable below 300 ft AGL in the pattern [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].
Can't land in the first third, or drifting while floating [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].
Excessive balloon or severe bounce [[24:204|AFH 9-33]] [[24:205|AFH 9-34]].
Any doubt about the landing surface [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]; first sign of wind shear [[28:266|AWH 22-11]].

body.p: LAHSO (land and hold short) means landing and stopping before an intersecting runway, taxiway, or a set point. Accept it only if you, as PIC, are sure you can land and stop within the Available Landing Distance (ALD), which is published in the Chart Supplement and Terminal Procedures [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]] [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. Student pilots and pilots not familiar with LAHSO should not participate, and the PIC has final authority to accept or decline [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. Plan it before the flight: know the ALD and slope for each combination at your destination [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]].

bullets: Declining? Tell ATC promptly, ideally before the clearance is issued [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].
Once accepted, comply like any clearance. A rejected landing is still allowed: keep clear of other traffic and notify the controller promptly [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].
Exit at the first convenient taxiway before the hold-short point, or stop at it [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].
Read back with the words "HOLD SHORT OF ..." [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]] [[33:256|AIM 4-3-11]].
You should only get LAHSO with at least a 1,000 ft ceiling and 3 statute miles visibility [[33:256|AIM 4-3-11]].

check.q: You accepted LAHSO, then balloon badly in the flare. May you go around, and what then?
check.a: Yes. LAHSO does not preclude a rejected landing. Keep safe separation from other traffic and tell the controller promptly [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]] [[24:204|AFH 9-33]].

chunks.title: Traffic, radios, right runway, and distractions

body.p: Collision hazards: aircraft on final or landing have the right-of-way, but must not use it to force a landed aircraft off the runway. When two are landing, the lower one has it but must not cut in front of or overtake one on final [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]. The FAA discourages VFR straight-ins; if you fly one, announce 8 to 10 miles out and coordinate, and remember you have no special priority over pattern traffic [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11.1]]. Instrument-rated pilots: an instrument approach in VMC has no priority over VFR traffic either [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.3]]. If others are in the pattern, use the same runway they are using [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11]].
Blind spots: high wings block the view above, low wings below, and the worst case is a low wing above a high wing. Bank now and then to uncover blind spots in the pattern [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].

Radio calls at a non-towered airport: monitor CTAF and self-announce about 10 miles out [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.1]], then downwind, base, and "on final for runway [XX]" [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]]. Do not broadcast your sequence number, and avoid "to" and "for", which can be mistaken for numbers [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.1, 10.3]].

Right runway: wrong-surface landings come from unfamiliar airports, complacency or fatigue. Study the airport diagram ahead of time, check runway number and alignment on every final, use the moving map, and go around if in doubt [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

After landing: exit at the first available taxiway or as ATC instructs, never onto another runway without ATC authorization. You are clear once all parts of the airplane are past the runway holding position markings; then hold unless told otherwise [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].

Distractions: plan and sequence tasks early. Get ATIS or AWOS, set frequencies and run checklists well before the airport so your eyes can be outside [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. The first sign of overload is working harder but accomplishing less; a task-saturated pilot loses awareness and decides on incomplete information. Stop, think, slow down, and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Many accidents start with a minor problem, like a gauge reading wrong, that pulls attention away from flying [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

check.q: Why does the FAA discourage VFR straight-in landings, and what must you do if you fly one?
check.a: They increase midair collision risk. Announce 8 to 10 miles out, coordinate with pattern traffic, and remember you have no special priority [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11.1]].

body.p: AFH common errors in normal landings [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]: late landing checklist, poor drift correction on base, bad or skidding turn to final, unstable approach, not compensating for flaps, poor trim, using elevator alone, focusing too close or too far, touching down before landing attitude, too little back pressure after touchdown, excessive braking, and loss of control. Go-around errors include not recognizing the need, indecision, delay, abrupt or late power, wrong pitch, and climbing out of ground effect too soon [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. Crosswind errors include exceeding the demonstrated crosswind, poor drift correction, excessive sink from sideslip drag, touching down drifting or misaligned, and excessive speed [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

head: Problem
Fix
rows: Power and pitch together; never retract flaps. Any doubt: go around [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
Flaps, less power, lower nose; or a forward slip. Over 800 to 1,000 fpm sink is excessive [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
Add power now; if slow and low, go around [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Prompt power before the stall; land only if runway allows, else go around. Nose wheel hits first: go around [[24:202|AFH 9-31]] [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]
Ease into landing attitude as it settles; not down in the first third or drifting: go around [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]
Power to cushion; lower the upwind wing further as you slow; drifting or excessive: go around [[24:204|AFH 9-33]]
Go around: full power, keep straight, lower the nose to a safe climb attitude [[24:205|AFH 9-34]]
Smooth back pressure; go around if conditions permit [[24:206|AFH 9-35]]
Touchdown in a drift or crab
Use wing-low; drift brings side loads, gear damage and ground loops [[24:206|AFH 9-35]]

callout.text: A 6-inch free fall onto the runway is roughly a 340 fpm descent, and touchdown loads can reach three or four times the airplane's weight [[24:206|AFH 9-35]]. Hold it off; don't drop it in.

check.q: You flare late, the nose wheel hits first, and the nose bounces up. Land or go around?
check.a: Go around immediately; do not try to force it back onto the runway [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].

f1.caption: Figure 9-5. Stabilized approach. (AFH 9-5)
f1.alt: Airplane descending along a blue path toward a runway. A yellow line extends the descent angle to the aiming point near the threshold; the airplane then flares and touches down farther down the runway, with an orange arrow showing the distance traveled in the flare.

f2.caption: FIG 2-1-5. Precision Approach Path Indicator (PAPI). (AIM 2-1-2) Open circles are white lights; filled circles are red lights.
f2.alt: Five PAPI light rows next to runway outlines, left to right: four white lights; three white and one red; two white and two red; one white and three red; four red. The angle labels are cropped off.

f3.caption: Figure 17-7. Runway illusions. (PHAK 17-11)
f3.alt: Side and cockpit views comparing narrower and wider runways and downsloping and upsloping runways. Dotted yellow lines show the normal approach and red lines show the lower approach caused by narrow or upsloping runways and the higher approach caused by wide or downsloping runways.

f4.caption: Figure 9-15. Crabbed approach. (AFH 9-16)
f4.alt: High-wing airplane over runway 34 with wings level and its nose angled into a wind blowing from the right, so it tracks down the runway centerline.

f5.caption: Figure 9-16. Sideslip approach. (AFH 9-16)
f5.alt: High-wing airplane over runway 08 with its right (upwind) wing lowered into a wind from the right and its nose lined up with the runway centerline.

f6.caption: Figure 9-19. Crosswind component chart. (AFH 9-19)
f6.alt: Quarter-circle chart with wind angle lines from 0 to 90 degrees and wind velocity arcs from 10 to 60. The vertical axis is headwind component and the horizontal axis is crosswind component, both 0 to 70.

f7.caption: FIG 7-4-7. Vortex Movement in Ground Effect - Tailwind. (AIM 7-4-4)
f7.alt: Diagram of a jet's vortices: a tailwind pushes the vortices left behind at the touchdown point forward onto the runway, into the touchdown zone of a following small airplane.

scenario.title: Checkride at a narrow country runway
scenario.setup: You are on your commercial checkride in a single-engine airplane, arriving at a non-towered airport you have never used. Runway 30 is 3,200 ft long and 60 ft wide (you usually fly from a 150-ft-wide runway) and slopes uphill, with a PAPI on the left. AWOS: wind 330 at 14 gusting 22; light rain fell an hour ago. Your POH approach speed is 70 kt and the placarded demonstrated crosswind is 15 kt. A King Air has just made a touch-and-go on runway 30. The examiner says: "Normal landing, touch down on the aiming point markings." On CTAF, another pilot says he will land straight in on runway 12 because it is closer.

questions.q: What speed do you fly on final, and what window must you hold?
questions.a: Gust factor 22 - 14 = 8 kt; add half: 74 kt [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Hold 69 to 79 kt (ACS CA.IV.B.S7), and don't let it decay below 70 kt [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

questions.q: Is the crosswind within limits, and how do you fly it?
questions.a: The wind is 30 degrees off the runway. The chart gives about 7 kt of crosswind at 14 kt and about 11 kt at 22 kt, under the 15 kt demonstrated value [[24:190|AFH 9-19]]. Fly wing-low, with partial flaps if the POH allows [[24:186|AFH 9-15]] [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

questions.q: What do you do about the King Air's touch-and-go?
questions.a: Its vortices can settle and move along the runway. Wait at least 2 minutes before you land; extend your downwind if needed [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. A light crosswind can hold the upwind vortex in the touchdown zone [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]].

questions.q: Which illusions do you expect, and how do you guard against them?
questions.a: The narrow runway and the upslope both make you feel higher than you are, so you will tend to fly low and land short [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]. Fly the PAPI and cross-check the altimeter [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].

questions.q: What is wrong with the other pilot's plan, and what do you do?
questions.a: Runway 12 gives him a tailwind of about 12 kt or more, and a 10 kt tailwind alone adds about 21% to landing distance [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.9]]; on a recently wet runway that is extra risky [[27:18|AC 91-79B 3.7]]. Opposite-direction traffic is also a collision risk. Announce your position and intentions on CTAF, keep scanning, and remind traffic to use the runway in use [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11]] [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.1]].

questions.q: At 200 ft the airspeed suddenly drops to 62 kt and you sink below the PAPI path. What now?
questions.a: Go around. You are 12 kt below your 74 kt target (ACS CA.IV.B.S7) and unstable below 300 ft [[24:177|AFH 9-6]], and a sudden airspeed loss can be wind shear [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. Power, attitude, then flaps up in steps [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

skills.do: Complete the before-landing checklist before base (gear down if retractable) and the after-landing checklist only when clear of the runway and stopped.
skills.practice: Tie the checklist to a fixed point on downwind and finish all briefings before the approach, so your eyes stay outside [[24:173|AFH 9-2]] [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

skills.do: Make CTAF position calls or tower calls as appropriate, and read back any hold-short clearance with the words "hold short of".
skills.practice: Chair-fly the 10-mile, downwind, base and final calls with no sequence numbers, and a full LAHSO readback [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]] [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

skills.do: Line up with the correct or assigned runway.
skills.practice: Study the airport diagram first; on every final, say the runway number out loud and check alignment and the moving map [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

skills.do: Scan the runway and adjoining area for traffic and obstructions.
skills.practice: Before turning final and again on short final, look at the runway, both ends, the taxiways and the final path, banking to uncover wing blind spots [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].

skills.do: Select and aim for a touchdown point suitable for the wind, surface and obstructions.
skills.practice: Name the aiming point and touchdown point before every landing, and learn your airplane's float using the aiming point and touchdown zone markings [[33:139|AIM 2-3-3]] [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].

skills.do: Set the recommended configuration, airspeed and trim, and adjust pitch and power together to stay stabilized.
skills.practice: Add flaps in steps and re-trim after each; use the PAPI or VASI to see path errors early [[24:173|AFH 9-2]] [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2]].

skills.do: Hold the published approach speed, or not more than 1.3 VSO, ±5 kt with gust factor applied (ACS CA.IV.B.S7).
skills.practice: Compute the target speed with the half-gust additive on downwind, then call out every deviation on final [[24:191|AFH 9-20]] [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

skills.do: Maintain directional control and correct crosswind correction through the approach, touchdown and rollout.
skills.practice: Practice the wing-low method on every crosswind day, increasing control inputs as you slow and holding full aileron into the wind as you stop [[24:187|AFH 9-16]] [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

skills.do: Make smooth, timely, correct control inputs in the round out and touchdown.
skills.practice: Start the round out at 10 to 20 ft, look ahead at 10 to 15 degrees, and hold the wheels just off the runway as long as possible [[24:178|AFH 9-7]] [[24:179|AFH 9-8]] [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].

skills.do: Touch down at a proper pitch attitude, on or within 200 ft beyond the specified point, with no side drift, aligned over the centerline (ACS CA.IV.B.S10).
skills.practice: Log where you touch down on every landing relative to a marked point; fix speed first, since excess speed causes float [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].

skills.do: Go around promptly when the approach is out of tolerance or unsafe: power, attitude, configuration.
skills.practice: Have your instructor call surprise go-arounds, including very close to the runway, and brief your go-around triggers before each flight [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Brief the exit before landing; exit at the first available taxiway, never onto another runway without ATC, and stop once past the holding position markings [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].

quiz.q: POH approach speed 70 kt, wind calm. Which airspeed range on final meets the commercial standard?
options: 65 to 75 kt
60 to 80 kt
65 to 80 kt
68 to 72 kt
quiz.why: The commercial ACS allows the published speed ±5 kt with gust factor applied (ACS CA.IV.B.S7). The AFH stabilized window of +10/-5 KIAS [[24:177|AFH 9-6]] is wider, so fly to the tighter ACS standard.

quiz.q: The examiner picks the runway aiming point markings as your point. About how far from the threshold is the latest touchdown that still meets the commercial standard?
quiz.why: The aiming point marking is about 1,000 ft from the threshold [[33:139|AIM 2-3-3]], and the ACS allows up to 200 ft beyond the point (ACS CA.IV.B.S10). 1,400 ft would be the private 400-ft standard.

quiz.q: A 4-light PAPI shows two white and two red lights. You are:
options: Slightly high, about 3.2 degrees
On the glide path, about 3 degrees
Slightly low, about 2.8 degrees
Low, under 2.5 degrees
quiz.why: Two white and two red means on the glide path, typically 3 degrees [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2]].

quiz.q: You land on a runway much narrower than you are used to. If you don't recognize the illusion, you tend to:
options: Fly a lower approach and risk landing short
Fly a higher approach and land long
Flare late and land nose first
Fly the normal path but too fast
quiz.why: A narrower-than-usual runway makes you feel higher than you are, so you fly a lower approach and risk hitting objects or landing short [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

quiz.q: POH approach speed 68 kt. Wind 190 at 9 gusting 21. Using the common AFH rule of thumb, your target speed is:
options: 68 kt
74 kt
80 kt
89 kt
quiz.why: Gust factor 21 - 9 = 12 kt. Add half: 68 + 6 = 74 kt [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. 80 kt adds the whole gust factor.

quiz.q: You cross the threshold at 80 ft instead of the 50 ft the POH assumes. About how much extra landing distance will you use?
options: 150 ft
300 ft
600 ft
quiz.why: Each 10 ft above 50 ft adds about 200 ft. 30 ft extra = 3 x 200 = 600 ft [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]].

quiz.q: Using the wing-low method with a crosswind from the right, you hold:
options: Left aileron (left wing low) and right rudder
Wings level and left rudder
Right aileron (right wing low) and left rudder
Right aileron and right rudder
quiz.why: Lower the upwind (right) wing to stop the drift and use opposite (left) rudder to keep the nose on centerline [[24:187|AFH 9-16]] [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

quiz.q: A larger airplane departing on a crossing runway rotates after passing your runway's intersection. What does the AIM recommend?
options: Go around and wait 2 minutes
Continue and land before the intersection
Land past the intersection
Fly below its flight path
quiz.why: If the departing aircraft rotates past the intersection, continue the approach and land prior to the intersection [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

quiz.q: What is the minimum weather for receiving a LAHSO clearance?
options: 500 ft ceiling and 1 statute mile
1,000 ft ceiling and 3 statute miles
1,500 ft ceiling and 5 statute miles
3,000 ft ceiling and 5 statute miles
quiz.why: Pilots should only receive LAHSO with at least a 1,000 ft ceiling and 3 statute miles visibility [[33:256|AIM 4-3-11]].

takeaways: Commercial windows: published speed (or not over 1.3 VSO) ±5 kt with gust factor applied, and touchdown on or within 200 ft past the point.
Stabilized by 500 ft in VMC (1,000 ft in IMC); unstable below 300 ft in the pattern means go around now.
Pitch and power move together; never fix a low approach with elevator alone or by raising flaps.
Use the PAPI/VASI or the 3-to-1 rule; narrow, upsloping and dark approaches make you fly low.
Wing-low, with more control as you slow; upwind main first; full aileron into the wind as you stop.
Speed, height, tailwind and slope add up: 10% fast is about 20% more runway, 10 kt tailwind about 21%.
Wake: above its path, beyond its touchdown. Go-around: power, attitude, configuration.
cfi_notes: The big change from private is the tolerance: ±5 kt instead of +10/-5, and 200 ft instead of 400 ft (ACS CA.IV.B.S7 and S10 vs PA.IV.B.S7 and S10). Most 200-ft misses are speed problems that show up as float [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].
The AFH stabilized criteria allow +10/-5 KIAS [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. That is a go/no-go gate for stabilization, not the commercial checkride standard; teach the ACS window.

The PHAK says both that a 10% excess landing speed causes 'at least a 21 percent' increase and that a 10% speed increase gives 20% [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. The newer AC 91-79B uses 20% [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]]; teach 20% and expect either on a test.

PHAK 12-11 still points students to AC 00-54 for wind shear [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. That AC is not in this course's sources; teach wind shear from AWH chapter 22 [[28:266|AWH 22-11]] [[28:273|AWH 22-18]].

Without a crosswind on checkride day, crosswind is tested orally (ACS CA.IV.B note). Drill the component chart, the 0.2 VSO idea and the 'full rudder can't stop the turn' limit [[24:190|AFH 9-19]] [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].
Have the student brief go-around triggers out loud before every pattern session; tie hesitation to landing expectancy and pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Take students to a narrow or sloping runway with a PAPI so they see the illusions for themselves [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]] [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2]].
gaps: Airplane-specific approach speeds, flap settings, demonstrated crosswind, checklists and landing distance and tailwind data are in the POH/AFM, not these resources.
The ACS does not define 'gust factor' or say exactly how to apply it; this lesson uses the AFH half-the-gust-factor practice (AFH 9-20) and treats the adjusted speed as the ±5 kt target.

No step-by-step wind shear escape procedure for small airplanes was found; AWH chapter 22 encounter studies involve large crew-flown airplanes. Get airplane-specific technique from the POH/AFM and your CFI.
The sources give no numbers for spot-landing technique (how far to place the aiming point before the touchdown point, or typical float distance); that comes from flight instruction in your airplane.
LAHSO Available Landing Distances and runway slope for specific airports are in the Chart Supplement and Terminal Procedures, which are not among these resources.

activities.title: Stable, or go around?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: 400 ft AGL in VMC: on path, on speed, in trim, 700 fpm
Banking 10 degrees on final to hold centerline in gusts
Power above the AFM minimum for approach, flaps set
900 fpm at 700 ft AGL, easing it below 500 fpm before 300 ft
Still setting flaps and running checklists at 400 ft AGL in VMC
Broke out of IMC, still not stabilized at 800 ft above the airport
Airspeed 8 kt below the AFM speed at 250 ft AGL
Piston trainer: approach goes unstable at 200 ft AGL

activities.why: The AFH criteria: constant 3-degree path, bank normally 15 degrees or less on final, +10/-5 KIAS, landing configuration in trim, 500 to 1,000 fpm (reduce below 500 before 300 ft if higher), power not below the AFM minimum, checklists done before the approach. Go around if not stabilized by 500 ft in VMC or 1,000 ft in IMC, and immediately if a piston approach goes unstable below 300 ft AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

activities.title: Work out your approach speeds
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Your airplane has no published approach speed. VSO is 52 kt. What is the highest final approach speed the AFH and ACS allow (1.3 VSO), to the nearest knot?
POH approach speed 70 kt. Wind 250 at 18 gusting 28. Using half the gust factor, what is your target speed?
items.why: Gust factor 28 - 18 = 10 kt. Half is 5: 70 + 5 = 75 kt [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

items.q: Your target with the gust additive is 75 kt. What is the lowest airspeed that still meets the commercial ±5 kt standard?
items.why: 75 - 5 = 70 kt (ACS CA.IV.B.S7). That is also the POH speed, which the AFH says not to decay below when using a gust factor [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

items.q: VSO is 55 kt. What base-leg target speed does the AFH suggest (1.4 VSO)?

activities.title: Read the PAPI
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin. Open circles are white lights; filled circles are red.
activities.why: Four white is high, three white and one red slightly high, two and two on the glide path, one white and three red slightly low, four red low [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2]].

activities.title: True or false: crosswind landings
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: The crab method may be easier to hold on final, but it needs precise timing to remove the crab before touchdown.
cards.why: Yes. That is why the AFH recommends wing-low in most cases [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

cards.s: Using wing-low, you level the wings in the flare so both mains touch at once.
cards.why: No. Keep the upwind wing down through the round out; the upwind main touches first [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

cards.s: With rudder-linked nose wheel steering, relax the corrective rudder as the nose wheel touches down.
cards.why: Yes. Otherwise the offset nose wheel makes the airplane swerve [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

cards.s: Once side load builds while drifting, firm braking is the best way to prevent a roll-over.
cards.why: No. Ailerons, rudder or steerable nose wheel may prevent it, but not brakes [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

cards.s: As little as 10 degrees of cornering angle can create a side load equal to half the weight on that tire.
cards.why: Yes. Above 20 degrees the side load stops increasing [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

cards.s: The placarded demonstrated crosswind is the airplane's certified maximum crosswind limit.
cards.why: No. Most airplanes give only a demonstrated crosswind, not a maximum limit [[27:19|AC 91-79B 3.10]]; it comes from certification testing to at least 0.2 VSO [[24:190|AFH 9-19]].

cards.s: Excessive sink or too low an airspeed from sideslip drag is a common crosswind landing error.
cards.why: Yes. It is on the AFH list of common crosswind errors [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

activities.title: Wind, height, and runway math
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Runway 27. Wind 300 at 20 kt. Using the crosswind component chart (30-degree angle), about how many knots of crosswind?
items.why: Follow the 30-degree line to the 20-kt arc and read down: about 10 kt crosswind (and about 17 kt headwind) [[24:190|AFH 9-19]].

items.q: POH landing distance (over a 50 ft obstacle) is 1,400 ft. You cross the threshold at 90 ft. About how much total distance will you need?
POH landing distance is 2,000 ft. You fly final 10% faster than the POH speed. About how much distance will you need?
Using the 3-to-1 rule (3,000 ft at 10 miles), what height above touchdown should you be at 3 miles out?
items.why: 3,000 ft at 10 miles is 300 ft per mile: 3 x 300 = 900 ft [[34:153|AIM 7-4-8]].

items.q: Your main tires are inflated to 25 psi. About what is the minimum dynamic hydroplaning speed?
items.why: 9 x square root of 25 = 9 x 5 = 45 kt [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]].

activities.title: Wake turbulence numbers
activities.intro: Tap an item, then the fact that goes with it.

pairs.r: Conditions that make the strongest vortices
How fast vortices sink behind a large aircraft
Sideways drift speed of vortices near the ground
Can hold the upwind vortex in the touchdown zone
Landing point from runway end behind a heavy jet
Wait after a larger aircraft's touch-and-go

activities.why: Heavy, clean, slow [[34:147|AIM 7-4-3]]; sink rate and 2 to 3 knot lateral drift [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]]; 1 to 5 knot crosswind [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]]; 1,000 ft landing point [[34:153|AIM 7-4-8]]; 2-minute interval [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

activities.title: Checkride landing at a Class D field
activities.intro: You are flying N52CA, a single-engine airplane, on your commercial checkride into a towered airport in Class D airspace. POH approach speed 65 kt; demonstrated crosswind 15 kt. Weather 4,500 broken, visibility 10 miles. ATIS: wind 230 at 12 gusting 20, runway 21. Your landing distance with a 15% margin is 1,700 ft. You have studied this airport's LAHSO combinations.

steps.s: On downwind you set your final approach target speed.
options: 65 kt, since gusts don't change approach speed
69 kt, half the 8-kt gust factor added
75 kt, the full gust value added
85 kt, to stay well above any stall
steps.why: Gust factor 20 - 12 = 8 kt; half is 4: 65 + 4 = 69 kt [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Your window is then 64 to 74 kt (ACS CA.IV.B.S7).

steps.s: Tower: "N52CA, runway 21, cleared to land, hold short of runway 15." The published ALD to runway 15 is 3,200 ft.
options: Read back: "Cleared to land runway 21, hold short of runway 15, N52CA"
Read back only "cleared to land 21" to save time
Accept, and plan to roll through runway 15 if you land long
Refuse, since LAHSO is never allowed on a checkride
steps.why: You may accept if you can land and stop within the ALD; 1,700 ft fits in 3,200 ft, and the weather is above 1,000 and 3 [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]] [[33:256|AIM 4-3-11]]. Read it back with "hold short of" and comply once accepted [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

steps.s: At 600 ft AGL on final, the PAPI shows one white and three red. Airspeed is 69 kt.
options: Lower the nose to gain a little speed
Add power and raise the nose together until you see two white and two red
Raise the flaps one notch to cut drag
Continue; the PAPI is only advisory in VFR
steps.why: One white, three red is slightly low [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2]]. In Class D you must stay at or above a visual approach slope indicator's glide path [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(e)(3)]]. Fix a low approach with power and pitch together, never by raising flaps [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

steps.s: Back on the path. At 150 ft the airspeed suddenly drops to 57 kt and the sink rate increases.
options: Pull the nose up to stay on the PAPI
Add a little power and continue; the box is still makeable
Go around now: power, then attitude, then configuration
Add full flaps for more lift
steps.why: 57 kt is well below your 64 to 74 kt window (ACS CA.IV.B.S7), a sudden airspeed loss may be wind shear [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]], and an approach unstable below 300 ft calls for an immediate go-around [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]: power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

steps.s: Full power is in. You are climbing slowly at 200 ft with full flaps, under your LAHSO clearance.
options: Raise all the flaps at once to climb faster
Raise the flaps in small steps as speed builds, keep clear of traffic, and tell the tower
Turn and land on runway 15 instead
Reduce power to stay below crossing traffic
steps.why: Retract flaps in small increments so the airplane accelerates; a sudden full retraction can make it settle back [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. After a rejected LAHSO landing, keep safe separation and notify the controller promptly [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane has no published approach speed and VSO is 48 kt. What is the highest final approach speed the ACS allows, before the ±5 kt tolerance?
options: 58 kt
62 kt
67 kt
72 kt
final_quiz.why: Not more than 1.3 VSO (ACS CA.IV.B.S7): 1.3 x 48 = 62.4, about 62 kt [[24:174|AFH 9-3]]. 67 kt is 1.4 VSO, the base-leg target [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

final_quiz.q: On a truly stabilized approach, how does the runway image change as you close in?
options: It gets shorter and wider
It gets longer and narrower
The aiming point moves down toward the nose
It keeps the same shape but grows larger
final_quiz.why: During a stabilized approach the runway shape does not change; it just gets proportionally larger. Shorter and wider means too shallow; longer and narrower means too steep [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].

final_quiz.q: You fly an instrument approach in IMC and break out on final. By what height above airport elevation should the approach have been stabilized?
options: 500 ft
300 ft
200 ft
final_quiz.why: Typically go around if not stabilized by 1,000 ft above airport elevation in IMC (500 ft in VMC) [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

final_quiz.q: You are landing at an airport in Class D airspace on a runway with a VASI. What does 14 CFR 91.129 require?
options: Fly the VASI only at night
Stay at least 1,500 ft above the airport until final
Stay at or above the glide path until lower is needed to land safely
Stay exactly on the glide path with no bracketing
final_quiz.why: You must maintain an altitude at or above the glide path until a lower altitude is necessary for a safe landing; normal bracketing is allowed [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(e)(3)-(4)]]. The 1,500 ft rule applies to large or turbine-powered airplanes.

final_quiz.q: POH landing distance is 1,800 ft. The only runway gives a 10 kt tailwind. About how much distance will you need, before any safety margin?
Short final, wing-low into a strong right crosswind. Even with full left rudder, the airplane keeps turning right. What is the right call?
options: Go around and land on a more favorable runway or at another airport
Level the wings and land in a crab
Add right rudder to help the turn stop
Land faster with the flaps up
final_quiz.why: If full opposite rudder cannot stop the turn at the bank you need, the wind is too strong for that runway; land on a more favorable runway or at an alternate [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

final_quiz.q: You are on a visual approach behind a heavy jet, with the jet and the runway in sight. Which practice does the AIM recommend?
options: Stay a few hundred feet below its path
Aim for the jet's exact touchdown point
Aim at the threshold to land well short of it
Aim no less than 1,000 ft down the runway, sighting above and ahead of the jet
final_quiz.why: Pick a landing point no less than 1,000 ft from the arrival end, with a line of sight that stays above and in front of the heavier aircraft, and fly on or above its glide path [[34:153|AIM 7-4-8]].

final_quiz.q: Which statement about microbursts on approach is correct, according to the Aviation Weather Handbook?
options: A headwind gain always warns you before the tailwind
Any microburst can be flown through at full power
Because they can be lopsided, the airspeed gain may be small or missing
Downdrafts are strongest right at the surface
final_quiz.why: Microbursts are often asymmetric, so the airspeed gain may be small or absent [[28:266|AWH 22-11]] [[28:273|AWH 22-18]]. Some cannot be escaped [[28:266|AWH 22-11]], and vertical winds usually peak above 500 ft [[28:273|AWH 22-18]].

final_quiz.q: During a go-around in a retractable-gear single, why are the flaps normally raised (at least partly) before the gear?
options: Full flaps make more drag than the gear, and gear down protects you if you touch down
The gear motor needs the flaps up to work
Raising the gear first pitches the nose down
The flaps must be fully up before any climb begins
final_quiz.why: On most airplanes full flaps make more drag than the gear, and if you touch down while starting the go-around you want the gear down and locked [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: Your main tires are inflated to 30 psi. About what is the minimum dynamic hydroplaning speed?
options: 54 kt
49 kt
45 kt
39 kt
final_quiz.why: 9 x square root of 30 = 9 x 5.48 = about 49 kt [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]]. 54 kt is the answer for 36 psi.

final_quiz.q: On short final you notice a gauge reading oddly and start troubleshooting it. What does the PHAK warn about this?
options: Gauge checks are required on short final
Fixing the gauge first is always safest
Minor problems lead to accidents when they pull attention from flying
The landing checklist must be redone first
final_quiz.why: Many distractions begin as a minor problem, such as a gauge reading wrong, and end in accidents when the pilot neglects control of the airplane [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

final_quiz.q: You balloon slightly in a gusty right crosswind. As the airplane settles back at a lower airspeed, what must you do?
options: Level the wings to land on both mains
Add left aileron to stop the drift
Release the rudder and let the nose weathervane
Lower the right wing more and hold left rudder
final_quiz.why: After a balloon the slower airplane drifts more, so lower the upwind wing further and hold opposite rudder; if in doubt or drifting, go around [[24:204|AFH 9-33]].

final_quiz.q: After landing at a towered airport with no taxi instructions, when is your airplane clear of the runway?
options: When all parts are past the runway holding position markings
When the nose wheel reaches the taxiway centerline
When the airplane passes the runway edge line
When you switch to ground control
final_quiz.why: You are clear when all parts of the airplane are past the runway edge and beyond the holding position markings; then hold unless instructed [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].
